title: General Relativity and Quantum Gravity
lead: General relativity extends Einstein’s ideas to accelerated motion and gravity, and its predictions reach from starlight bent by the Sun to black holes and waves in space itself. This section follows those predictions and the evidence for them, and closes on quantum gravity, the theory still sought for places where gravity acts on the quantum scale.
objectives: Explain the effect of gravity on light.
summary_html:
• Einstein’s theory of general relativity includes accelerated frames and, thus, encompasses special relativity and gravity. Created by use of careful thought experiments, it has been repeatedly verified by real experiments.
  • One direct result of this behavior of nature is the gravitational lensing of light by massive objects, such as galaxies, also seen in the microlensing of light by smaller bodies in our galaxy.
  • Another prediction is the existence of black holes, objects for which the escape velocity is greater than the speed of light and from which nothing can escape.
  • The event horizon is the distance from the object at which the escape velocity equals the speed of light $\kc$. It is called the Schwarzschild radius $\kRS$ and is given by $$\kRS = \frac{2G\kM}{\kc^{2}}\text{,}$$ where $G$ is the universal gravitational constant, and $\kM$ is the mass of the body.
  • Physics is unknown inside the event horizon, and the possibility of wormholes and time travel are being studied.
  • Candidates for black holes may power the extremely energetic emissions of quasars, distant objects that seem to be early stages of galactic evolution.
  • Neutron stars are stellar remnants, having the density of a nucleus, that hint that black holes could form from supernovas, too.
  • Gravitational waves are wrinkles in space, predicted by general relativity but not yet observed, caused by changes in very massive objects.
  • Quantum gravity is an incompletely developed theory that strives to include general relativity, quantum mechanics, and unification of forces (thus, a TOE).
  • One unconfirmed connection between general relativity and quantum mechanics is the prediction of characteristic radiation from just outside black holes.

figures.original_caption: (a) A beam of light emerges from a flashlight in an upward-accelerating elevator. Since the elevator moves up during the time the light takes to reach the wall, the beam strikes lower than it would if the elevator were not accelerated. (b) Gravity has the same effect on light, since it is not possible to tell whether the elevator is accelerating upward or acted upon by gravity.

This schematic shows how light passing near a massive body like the Sun is curved toward it. The light that reaches the Earth then seems to be coming from different locations than the known positions of the originating stars. Not only was this effect observed, the amount of bending was precisely what Einstein predicted in his general theory of relativity.

Gravity and quantum mechanics come into play when a black hole creates a particle-antiparticle pair from the energy in its gravitational field. One member of the pair falls into the hole while the other escapes, removing energy and shrinking the black hole. The search is on for the characteristic energy.

referents.label: the elevator at rest in a gravitational field
the star whose light the Sun bends

exercises.prompt: Quantum gravity, if developed, would be an improvement on both general relativity and quantum mechanics, but more mathematically difficult. Under what circumstances would it be necessary to use quantum gravity? Similarly, under what circumstances could general relativity be used? When could special relativity, quantum mechanics, or classical physics be used?

answer.solution: Quantum gravity is needed only where gravity is so strong that it acts on the quantum scale: in the earliest moments of the universe, and just outside the event horizon of a black hole, where particle-antiparticle pairs are created. General relativity serves wherever gravity is strong or there is acceleration but quantum effects do not matter: light bent by the Sun, lensing by galaxies, the event horizon itself, gravitational waves. Special relativity serves where there is no acceleration and gravity is weak but relative speeds approach the speed of light. Quantum mechanics serves on the atomic and subatomic scale, where gravity is negligible. Classical physics serves where speeds are small compared with the speed of light, objects are large compared with atoms, and gravity is weak.

exercises.prompt: Does observed gravitational lensing correspond to a converging or diverging lens? Explain briefly.

answer.solution: A converging lens. Gravity bends light toward the mass, so rays passing on either side of an intervening galaxy are bent inward, toward one another, as a converging lens bends rays toward its axis. That is how light from a distant galaxy reaches the Earth along several paths and forms several images.

exercises.prompt: Suppose you measure the red shifts of all the images produced by gravitational lensing, such as in Figure 34.12. You find that the central image has a red shift less than the outer images, and those all have the same red shift. Discuss how this not only shows that the images are of the same object, but also implies that the red shift is not affected by taking different paths through space. Does it imply that cosmological red shifts are not caused by traveling through space (light getting tired, perhaps)?

answer.solution: Images with one spectrum and one red shift, which also brighten and dim together, are one object seen along several paths. The central image is the nearer, intervening galaxy, and its smaller red shift fits its smaller distance. The outer images reached us along different paths, passing different sides of that galaxy, yet arrived with the same red shift, so the path the light took does not change it: the red shift is set by the source. This argues against light getting tired along the way, but only weakly, since the paths differ in length by a tiny fraction of the whole distance; it is consistent with red shift caused by the expansion of the universe, without ruling the alternative out on its own.

exercises.prompt: What are gravitational waves, and have they yet been observed either directly or indirectly?

answer.solution: Gravitational waves are distortions in space created by moving masses, predicted by general relativity, that travel at the speed of light. They were observed indirectly by Taylor and Hulse, who found the orbit of a binary neutron star system changing precisely as general relativity predicts for a system radiating gravitational wave energy. They were observed directly on September 14, 2015 by the twin LIGO detectors, and in 2016 LIGO and VIRGO announced the first confirmed observation of gravitational waves from colliding black holes.

exercises.prompt: Is the event horizon of a black hole the actual physical surface of the object?

answer.solution: No. The event horizon is the distance from the object at which the escape velocity equals the speed of light, a radius $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$. It is the boundary inside which nothing, not even light, can get out, not a material surface: the object itself lies inside the event horizon.

exercises.prompt: Suppose black holes radiate their mass away and the lifetime of a black hole created by a supernova is about $10^{67}$ years. How does this lifetime compare with the accepted age of the universe? Is it surprising that we do not observe the predicted characteristic radiation?

answer.solution: The universe is roughly $10^{10}$ years old, so a lifetime of $10^{67}$ years is some $10^{57}$ times longer: a black hole made in a supernova has barely begun to evaporate. Its radiation is extremely feeble and its final burst lies unimaginably far in the future, so it is not surprising that the characteristic radiation has not been observed. Only much smaller black holes, perhaps left over from the Big Bang, could be evaporating now, and searches for their characteristic γ-ray bursts have so far found more mundane sources.

exercises.prompt: What is the Schwarzschild radius of a black hole that has a mass eight times that of our Sun? Note that stars must be more massive than the Sun to form black holes as a result of a supernova.

answer.hint: Put eight times the Sun’s mass, $1.99\times 10^{30}\;\text{kg}$, into $R_{\text{S}} = 2GM/c^{2}$.

exercises.prompt: Supermassive black holes are thought to exist at the center of many galaxies. (a) What is the radius of such an object if it has a mass of $10^{9}$ Suns? (b) What is this radius in light years?

parts.hint: A light year is the distance light travels in one year, about $9.46\times 10^{15}\;\text{m}$.

exercises.prompt: The core of a star collapses during a supernova, forming a neutron star. Angular momentum of the core is conserved, and so the neutron star spins rapidly. If the initial core radius is $5.0\times 10^{5}\;\text{km}$ and it collapses to 10.0 km, find the neutron star’s angular velocity in revolutions per second, given the core’s angular velocity was originally 1 revolution per 30.0 days.

answer.hint: Treat the core before and after as a uniform sphere, $I = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^{2}$, and set $I\omega$ before equal to $I\omega$ after.
